content: The two included trials investigated the effects of interventions on the incidence of mastitis within six months postpartum. Two comparisons were made: (1) oral prophylactic antibiotics versus placebo or usual care, and (2) topical prophylactic antibiotics versus placebo or no intervention. The evidence and judgments regarding the effects of these interventions (desirable effects, undesirable effects, and certainty of the evidence) were presented separately for each comparison. Comparison 1: Oral prophylactic antibiotics versus placebo or usual care Comparison 1a: Oral antibiotics (flucloxacillin) versus placebo This comparison included one trial conducted in Australia in 2004, involving 10 lactating women with cracked nipples colonized by Staphylococcus aureus. The trial compared oral flucloxacillin (administered for seven days) with placebo capsules for the same duration. The trial was terminated early due to poor compliance with the intervention and a lack of eligible participants. Maternal functioning, well-being, and adverse effects were not reported in this trial. Additionally, health service use and postnatal care experiences were not addressed in the systematic review. Breastfeeding status and adverse effects in newborns/infants were also not reported. Comparison 1b: Oral antibiotics (cloxacillin/erythromycin) versus usual care (breastfeeding advice) This comparison included data from a four-arm trial conducted in Canada in 1999, involving 84 women attending a breastfeeding clinic for issues such as cracked/sore nipples or positive S. aureus results. The trial compared four groups: topical 2% mupirocin ointment applied to the nipples (25 women), topical fusidic acid ointment applied to the nipples (17 women), oral antibiotics (cloxacillin/erythromycin, regimen not reported) with breastfeeding advice (19 women), and breastfeeding advice alone (23 women). The trial was stopped early because the authors perceived a higher rate of mastitis in women who did not receive antibiotics, although no further information was provided. Maternal functioning, well-being, and adverse effects were not reported. Health service use and postnatal care experiences were also not addressed. Breastfeeding status and adverse effects in newborns/infants were not reported. Comparison 2: Topical prophylactic antibiotics versus usual care (breastfeeding advice) This comparison included data from the third arm of the four-arm trial described above. The evidence suggested that topical prophylactic antibiotics may make little or no difference to the incidence of mastitis within six months postpartum compared to usual care. Maternal functioning, well-being, and adverse effects were not reported. Health service use and postnatal care experiences were also not addressed. Breastfeeding status and adverse effects in newborns/infants were not reported. Additional Considerations A Cochrane systematic review updated in 2020 on treatments for breast engorgement during lactation included 21 trials (2,170 women). While mastitis was a pre-specified outcome, none of the trials included mastitis as an outcome. A 2013 Cochrane review on antibiotic therapies for breastfeeding women with mastitis found insufficient evidence to confirm or refute the effectiveness of antibiotics for lactational mastitis. Findings from a qualitative evidence synthesis highlighted the importance some women place on breastfeeding as a means of bonding with their baby and the challenges they face when breastfeeding is difficult or painful. Women may welcome additional support, information, and treatment to facilitate successful breastfeeding. However, many women may prefer to avoid the inconvenience and adverse effects of antibiotics. Health workers and policymakers are likely to value the potential impact of antibiotic use on resistance, and there may be no variation in this value across settings. No economic evaluations of pharmacological interventions for preventing mastitis were identified. Prophylactic antibiotics may increase equity due to their low cost and wide availability but could decrease equity if women are expected to pay for them. Breastfeeding rates are suboptimal worldwide, particularly among low-income women. Increasing breastfeeding initiation and duration, including preventing breast problems that may affect continuation, could improve health outcomes for mothers and infants while reducing economic burdens. WHO Recommendations on Postpartum Constipation Prevention Dietary advice and information on factors associated with constipation should be provided to women to prevent postpartum constipation. This includes promoting a healthy, balanced diet with adequate water and dietary fiber intake (e.g., vegetables, fruits, nuts, and whole grains) and encouraging physical activity (e.g., walking for at least 150 minutes per week). Constipation during the postpartum period may result from various factors, including hematinics used during pregnancy, disrupted eating and drinking during labor, enemas, narcotic drugs administered during labor or post-cesarean birth, perineal pain, irregular dietary patterns, and psychosocial factors. Prevention should address these underlying factors. Routine use of laxatives for preventing postpartum constipation is not recommended. A stepwise approach should be applied, where laxatives are used only if dietary modifications or fiber supplementation fail to relieve constipation. This approach should be applied throughout the postpartum period, after both vaginal and cesarean births. Women should be asked about their bowel movements during their postpartum stay in health facilities and at each postnatal care contact. They should receive dietary advice and information on factors associated with constipation. Further investigation into the effects of routine laxative use for preventing postpartum constipation is not considered a research priority. Evidence Summary on Laxative Use Data from four trials involving 1,061 women were included in a Cochrane review on interventions for preventing postpartum constipation. The trials, conducted in Ireland, South Africa, and the USA, were published over 40 years ago. All trials compared laxatives versus no intervention or placebo. The laxatives evaluated included bisoxatin acetate, active senna, Dorbanex, and dioctyl-sodium succinate plus senna. Bisoxatin acetate is now contraindicated for breastfeeding women, and Dorbanex is no longer available due to its carcinogenic potential. Only data from trials involving available and indicated treatments for postpartum women are described.
